exam: IISER Aptitude Test (IAT) 2027 preparation — provisional 2026-pattern pilot
title: IAT New Test 12
review_status: fresh AI-assisted authoring; independent academic review pending
notification_source: Official IAT 2026 examination page and 2026 Information Brochure, sections 19 and 23; a 2027 brochure has not been verified
past_paper_reference: 539 English archive entries from 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2021–2026; 2026 key provisional; analysed for topic/style only, no questions copied
authoring_source: Individually authored TSV records against the 25-test slot plan; mechanical assembly only; academic review pending
order_policy: fixed authored order; do not shuffle questions or options or renumber image-linked IDs
instructions: This is an original preparation pilot for manual review, based on the verified 2026 scheme; it is not an official IAT paper or a verified 2027 notification.
There are 60 single-correct questions: Biology 1–15, Chemistry 16–30, Mathematics 31–45 and Physics 46–60.
Each question has exactly one correct option. Correct: +4; incorrect: -1; unanswered: 0. All questions are available to attempt; there is no best-three-subject scoring rule.
Use 180 minutes. An on-screen non-programmable scientific calculator is part of the 2026 examination conditions; personal calculators are not allowed under that scheme.
Treat stated data and idealisations as exact unless an approximation is explicitly supplied. Log denotes base 10 and ln denotes the natural logarithm.
The review PDF contains the question paper first, followed by a separate answer key and worked solutions. Keep the solutions hidden during a timed attempt.

difficulty_policy.basis: user-directed editorial mix, not measured item difficulty

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In the pictured hierarchy, two organisms belong to the same genus but different species. Which is the narrowest rank they necessarily share?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Genus.
Why: Genus encloses multiple related species. Membership in one genus entails shared family and higher ranks, but the question asks for the narrowest guaranteed shared rank. Distinct species excludes species as a common assignment.
Why not the others: (B) family is shared but is not the narrowest known rank; (C) order is broader still; (D) species is explicitly different for P and Q.
Key point: Move upward from species only as far as necessary.
questions.image_alt: Taxonomic ranks relating species to genus and family

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.question: The section shows palisade mesophyll immediately beneath the upper epidermis and spongy mesophyll below. Light arrives from above. Which comparison is best supported?
options: A) Stomata can occur only on the upper epidermis
B) Upper palisade cells receive incident light before the deeper spongy layer
C) The spongy layer contains no chloroplasts
D) All mesophyll cells have identical exposure
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Upper palisade receives incident light first.
Why: The depicted vertical arrangement places the palisade layer between the illuminated surface and spongy tissue. It supports a light-exposure inference without claiming that deeper cells cannot photosynthesise.
Why not the others: (A) stomatal placement is not fixed by this section; (C) spongy cells also contain chloroplasts; (D) ignores the layer order.
Key point: Use the indicated geometry, not an invented absolute rule.
questions.image_alt: Upper palisade and lower spongy mesophyll under incident light

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A homogenate is centrifuged sequentially: intact nuclei sediment first; a later, higher-speed pellet contains double-membraned organelles with their own circular DNA. Which activity is most enriched in that later pellet?
options: B) Photosynthetic light reaction in every animal cell
C) Aerobic ATP synthesis in mitochondria
D) Translation on free cytosolic ribosomes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Mitochondrial aerobic ATP synthesis.
Why: Nuclear material was removed in the first pellet, while the second fraction is consistent with mitochondria, which are double membraned and have their own DNA. Enrichment means higher relative concentration, not exclusive localization.
Why not the others: (A) follows nuclei; (B) animal cells lack chloroplasts; (D) free ribosomes largely remain in supernatant.
Key point: Link sedimentation order to organelle structure and function.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A sealed thylakoid is kept in darkness. The lumen is pH 5 and the external medium pH 8; ADP and phosphate are outside, and the ATP-synthase head faces outward. What can initially occur if the membrane is proton-tight except through synthase?
options: B) CO₂ fixation without ATP or NADPH
C) Protons move from pH 8 to pH 5 through synthase
D) Protons exit the lumen and drive ATP production outside
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Lumen-to-outside proton flow can synthesize ATP.
Why: The lumen has greater hydrogen-ion concentration; a permitted path through ATP synthase releases stored gradient energy to phosphorylate external ADP. Darkness blocks a sustained photosynthetic gradient, but an imposed initial gradient can transiently drive ATP synthesis.
Why not the others: (A) requires light-driven water splitting; (B) ignores energy inputs; (C) reverses spontaneous diffusion.
Key point: Follow both concentration gradient and catalytic-head side.
questions.image_alt: Thylakoid proton gradient and ATP synthase orientation

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A transmitter is released normally, but a drug occupies postsynaptic receptors without opening the ion channel. Which observation best isolates the drug's action?
options: A) Directly faster axonal conduction in the postsynaptic neuron
B) No presynaptic action potential and no vesicle fusion
C) Higher postsynaptic potential with unchanged release
D) Normal presynaptic vesicle fusion but reduced postsynaptic potential
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Normal release with weak postsynaptic response.
Why: The premise preserves presynaptic release, so an impaired electrical response after receptor occupancy localizes the defect to receptor-mediated transduction at the postsynaptic membrane. A control of release distinguishes this from upstream failure.
Why not the others: (A) concerns propagation rather than the tested synapse; (B) changes the presynaptic premise; (C) predicts enhancement.
Key point: Separate transmitter release from receptor response.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A single megaspore mother cell forms four megaspores; only one survives and undergoes three mitoses before cellularisation. How many nuclei are present immediately before cellularisation in the surviving embryo sac?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Eight nuclei.
Why: Meiotic products are four separate megaspores, but only one functional megaspore continues. Each of its three mitotic rounds doubles nuclei: one becomes two, then four, then eight. Counting all original megaspores would overcount the developing sac.
Why not the others: (B) stops after two divisions; (C) adds an extra mitosis; (D) multiplies all four meiotic products.
Key point: Track only the functional megaspore after meiosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An autosomal recessive disease affects a child's sibling; both parents are unaffected obligate carriers. The child is unaffected. If this child has a partner known to be a carrier, what is the chance their first child is affected?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/6.
Given: Carrier parents Aa × Aa; unaffected child excludes aa.
Formula/Principle: Conditional carrier chance is 2/3; two carriers produce aa with probability 1/4.
Step 1: (2/3)(1/4)=1/6.
Why: Restrict the parental offspring distribution to AA and Aa after learning the person is unaffected. The affected sibling establishes parental genotypes but does not make the unaffected child certainly a carrier.
Why not the others: (A) assumes carrier status; (B) uses wrong conditional fraction; (D) gives carrier risk, not affected-offspring risk.
Key point: Condition on unaffected status before mating probability.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A rare resistance allele already exists in a bacterial culture before antibiotic is applied. Resistant colonies dominate afterward. Which inference is justified?
options: A) The antibiotic preferentially selected pre-existing resistant cells
B) The antibiotic intentionally created resistance in each survivor
C) All survivors acquired the allele from the drug molecule
D) Every initially sensitive bacterium must have mutated
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Selection changed allele frequencies.
Why: Pre-existing heritable variation and differential survival suffice to explain enrichment of resistance. The drug is the selecting environment, and the observation alone does not establish that it induced mutations in all survivors.
Why not the others: (B) assumes the drug deliberately creates a useful mutation; (C) treats an antibiotic molecule as an allele donor; (D) assumes every sensitive cell changed rather than dying.
Key point: Selection acts on variation already present.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The plasmid diagram marks a resistance gene R interrupted by the cloning site and an intact resistance gene S. A colony grows on S-antibiotic but fails on R-antibiotic after transformation. What is the most direct inference?
options: B) The inserted DNA disrupted S
D) An insert likely interrupted R while S remained functional
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Insertional inactivation of R.
Why: Growth with S-antibiotic supports the intact S marker and plasmid uptake; loss of R growth is consistent with a DNA insert disrupting R at the shown site. A control uncut vector would help exclude unrelated mutations.
Why not the others: (A) conflicts with S selection; (B) predicts loss of S growth; (C) predicts loss on both media.
Key point: Read each selection phenotype against its own gene.
questions.image_alt: Two resistance markers and the plasmid insertion site

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Two species consume the same limiting resource. Alone they persist at equal density; together A persists while B declines, but supplying abundant resource restores B. Which explanation best fits both observations?
options: A) A directly poisons B under all conditions
B) Predation by A is proved because B declines
C) B is genetically incapable of reproduction
D) Resource competition suppresses B when the shared resource is limiting
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Resource-mediated competition.
Why: The abundance intervention removes the limiting-resource condition and rescues B, providing evidence that resource depletion, rather than unavoidable toxicity, drives its decline in the mixed culture. Equal monoculture performance does not imply equal competitive ability.
Why not the others: (A) would persist after supplementation; (B) does not follow from resource rescue; (C) contradicts B alone.
Key point: A rescue treatment tests the proposed cause.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A heterozygote in coupling phase AB/ab is test-crossed. Among 1000 progeny, AB and ab each occur 390 times, while Ab and aB each occur 110 times. What is the map distance between the loci?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 22 cM.
Given: Test-cross progeny reveal heterozygote gametes; recombinants are Ab and aB.
Formula/Principle: Recombination fraction = recombinant total / total.
Step 1: (110+110)/1000=0.22, corresponding to 22 cM.
Why: Coupling phase makes AB and ab parental even though each is not half the sample; the smaller two classes identify recombination. This distance is an approximation from the observed two-locus fraction.
Why not the others: (A) counts one recombinant class; (C) counts one parental class; (D) sums the parentals.
Key point: Identify parental phase before summing recombinants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An X-linked recessive allele is present in a man whose partner is unaffected and homozygous normal. Which child class is obligatorily a carrier under ordinary XX/XY inheritance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) All daughters.
Why: The father gives his sole X chromosome to every daughter and his Y to every son. Each daughter also receives a normal maternal X, so she carries the allele without expressing a recessive trait under the stipulated genotype.
Why not the others: (A) incorrectly sends a paternal X to every son; (B) assigns that X to half the sons despite Y inheritance; (D) overlooks that every daughter receives the father's single X.
Key point: Trace paternal X and Y separately.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Thyroid hormone rises above its normal set point in a person with an intact hypothalamic-pituitary axis. What immediate feedback change is expected?
options: A) TRH and TSH decrease through negative feedback
B) TSH secretion increases to reinforce the rise
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Lower TRH and TSH.
Why: Elevated thyroid hormone inhibits hypothalamic TRH and anterior-pituitary TSH secretion, reducing stimulation of the thyroid gland. This is a reversible homeostatic response in the stated intact axis.
Why not the others: (B) is positive feedback; (C) asserts permanent damage; (D) confuses endocrine axes.
Key point: Increased final hormone suppresses upstream drive.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: At identical substrate concentration, enzyme velocity falls after adding compound X. Raising substrate concentration restores the original maximum rate, while the concentration required for half-maximal speed increases. Which model fits?
options: B) Noncompetitive inhibition lowering maximum rate
C) Competitive inhibition at the substrate site
D) Loss of enzyme molecules from the mixture
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Competitive inhibition.
Why: More substrate overcomes X, leaving the limiting maximum velocity unchanged but increasing apparent substrate requirement. The paired observations distinguish occupancy competition from reduced active enzyme amount.
Why not the others: (A) heat-denatured enzyme would not regain the same maximum with more substrate; (B) noncompetitive inhibition lowers maximum velocity; (D) fewer active enzyme molecules also lower maximum capacity.
Key point: Examine both limiting velocity and substrate dependence.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A leaf's photosynthetic rate rises with light up to a plateau at fixed CO₂. Increasing CO₂ at the plateau raises the rate, but only until a new plateau. What does this demonstrate?
options: A) Light can never limit photosynthesis
B) CO₂ was limiting at the first plateau, though another factor later limits
C) CO₂ is irrelevant to carbon fixation
D) The same factor must limit at every plateau
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Limitation can shift.
Why: A response to increased CO₂ at unchanged light shows that CO₂ supply constrained the first plateau. The second plateau shows that additional CO₂ no longer changes the rate there; light, temperature, enzyme capacity or another factor may now constrain it.
Why not the others: (A) ignores that light can limit at low intensity; (C) contradicts the observed CO₂ response; (D) assumes the same bottleneck persists despite the intervention.
Key point: Diagnose the limiting factor by changing one input.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure labels a carbon atom with one single C–C bond and one triple C≡N bond in CH₃–C≡N. What is the hybridisation of that carbon, and how many π bonds are incident on it?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) sp with two π bonds.
Why: The nitrile carbon has two electron-domain directions: one σ bond toward methyl and one σ component toward nitrogen. Linear sp hybrid orbitals form those σ bonds; its two unhybridised p orbitals form the two π components of the triple bond.
Why not the others: (A) counts single bonds only; (B) treats a triple bond as a double; (C) misses one π component.
Key point: A triple bond counts as one domain but has two π bonds.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The square-planar complex [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂] is shown with adjacent ligands on one sketch and opposite ligands on another. How many distinct geometrical arrangements exist, ignoring optical isomerism?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Two.
Why: The identical chlorides can be adjacent (cis) or opposite (trans) on a square plane. Rotating the square maps other drawings onto one of these two; swapping the ammine labels does not create another arrangement.
Why not the others: (A) counts one rotated cis/trans drawing as a third form; (B) counts both rotations as new forms; (C) fails to distinguish adjacent from opposite chloride placement.
Key point: Identify configurations modulo rotation.
questions.image_alt: Adjacent and opposite ligand arrangements on a square plane

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For the nitrate ion NO₃⁻, compare Lewis structures with one N=O and two N–O bonds to a hypothetical three N=O structure. Why is the latter inadmissible for second-period nitrogen?
options: A) Its oxygen atoms lack electrons
B) It assigns nitrogen more than an octet of electrons
C) It gives every oxygen a negative formal charge
D) It violates conservation of oxygen atoms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Nitrogen cannot exceed an octet here.
Why: Three N=O double bonds put 12 bonding electrons around central nitrogen, beyond the second-row octet. The valid resonance contributors have one double and two single bonds, with formal charges distributed over oxygen through resonance. Formal-charge minimisation cannot override the octet restriction.
Why not the others: (A) electron supply is not the limiting rule; (C) misstates charges; (D) keeps three oxygens.
Key point: Apply valence-shell restrictions before formal-charge ranking.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which proposed quantum-number set can describe an electron in an atomic orbital? Values are (n,l,m_l,m_s).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (4,2,−2,+1/2).
Why: For n=4, l can be 0 to 3, and l=2 permits m_l from −2 to +2; spin is ±1/2. All four numbers in the selected tuple meet these nested constraints.
Why not the others: (A) requires l<n; (B) has magnitude m_l greater than l; (D) uses spin +1 instead of ±1/2.
Key point: Check allowed ranges in sequence.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Under otherwise comparable conditions, which carbocation is most stabilised by resonance?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Allylic carbocation.
Why: The empty p orbital adjacent to the C=C bond can delocalise positive charge over the allylic framework. Alkyl substitution stabilises tertiary carbocations by other effects, but only the chosen structure has the requested resonance stabilisation.
Why not the others: (A) ethyl has no adjacent C=C π system; (B) tertiary alkyl substitution gives hyperconjugation rather than the specified resonance; (D) methyl has no neighboring π bond.
Key point: Distinguish resonance from hyperconjugation and induction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The two samples in the figure are ethanal (X) and propanone (Y). X gives Tollens silver; both X and Y give iodoform. Which conclusion follows?
options: A) Only X contains a methyl carbonyl group
C) Y is an aldehyde because iodoform is positive
D) Tollens distinguishes X as an aldehyde whereas iodoform is not specific for aldehydes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Different tests probe different structural features.
Why: Ethanal reduces Tollens reagent and has a CH₃CO– pattern; propanone has the methyl ketone pattern but is not an aldehyde, so it gives iodoform without Tollens silver under the stated test. Joint evidence separates carbonyl class from methyl-carbonyl response.
Why not the others: (A) wrongly excludes the methyl ketone Y from iodoform response; (B) treats a ketone as an aldehyde; (C) mistakes an iodoform-positive methyl ketone for an aldehyde.
Key point: A positive iodoform test does not uniquely identify an aldehyde.
questions.image_alt: Carbonyl structures of ethanal and propanone

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: At equal concentration in water, aniline is less basic than cyclohexylamine. Which structural effect most directly explains this comparison?
options: A) Aniline nitrogen's lone pair is delocalised into the aromatic ring
B) Cyclohexylamine's lone pair is delocalised into an aromatic ring
C) Aniline has no nitrogen lone pair
D) Both amines are identical after protonation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Aromatic lone-pair delocalisation.
Why: Delocalisation of aniline's unprotonated nitrogen lone pair reduces its availability to accept a proton. Cyclohexylamine lacks conjugation with an aromatic π system; the stipulated aqueous comparison is consistent with the difference.
Why not the others: (B) invents an aromatic ring; (C) contradicts nitrogen valence; (D) ignores different conjugate-acid structures and solvation.
Key point: Consider lone-pair availability in the specified solvent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Complete hydrolysis of the tripeptide Gly–Ala–Gly yields which products and mole ratio?
options: D) Only Gly, because terminal residues are removed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Two glycines per alanine.
Why: Hydrolysis breaks both peptide bonds without changing residue identity. The original sequence has glycine at both ends and alanine in the middle, yielding two moles of glycine and one mole of alanine per mole of peptide.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the counts; (C) ignores alanine; (D) treats bond cleavage as residue deletion.
Key point: Count residues before and after complete hydrolysis.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Initial-rate trials: [A],[B],rate = (0.10,0.10,2), (0.20,0.10,8), (0.10,0.20,4), with consistent units. What is the empirical rate law?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Second order in A, first in B.
Why: Doubling A at fixed B multiplies the rate by four, giving exponent 2. Doubling B at fixed A multiplies the rate by two, giving exponent 1. Initial rates establish an empirical law, not necessarily the molecularity of an elementary step.
Why not the others: (B) predicts fourfold for B; (C) predicts twofold for A; (D) reverses the observed exponents.
Key point: Compare one concentration change at a time.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: For AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺+Cl⁻, Ksp=10⁻¹⁰. In a solution already containing 0.01 M Cl⁻, and neglecting activity changes, what is the approximate molar solubility of AgCl?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 10⁻⁸ M.
Given: Background chloride 10⁻² M is much greater than anticipated dissolved AgCl.
Formula/Principle: Ksp=[Ag⁺][Cl⁻]≈s(10⁻²).
Step 1: s=10⁻¹⁰/10⁻²=10⁻⁸ M; added chloride from dissolution is negligible.
Why: The common ion fixes the chloride concentration approximately while each dissolved formula unit gives one Ag⁺. The Ag⁺ produced at this small solubility changes the 0.01 M background chloride by only about one part in a million, so the approximation is self-consistent.
Why not the others: (A) is pure-water solubility; (B) misplaces two powers; (C) treats Ksp as concentration.
Key point: Check the common-ion approximation afterward.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻ is reduced to Mn²⁺. How many electrons does one permanganate ion accept in the balanced half-reaction?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Five electrons.
Why: Mn changes oxidation state from +7 in MnO₄⁻ to +2 in Mn²⁺, so its reduction requires five electrons. Balancing oxygen as water and hydrogen as H⁺ does not change that electron count: MnO₄⁻+8H⁺+5e⁻→Mn²⁺+4H₂O.
Why not the others: (B) uses a three-electron count without the Mn oxidation-state difference; (C) imports the +7 oxidation state as the electron count; (D) uses the final +2 state instead of the difference.
Key point: Electron count equals the central atom's oxidation-state decrease.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A reaction has ΔH>0 and ΔS>0, both approximately temperature independent in the relevant interval. Which temperature condition permits ΔG<0?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Above the threshold.
Why: ΔG=ΔH−TΔS. Both terms are positive initially, but the entropy term grows with temperature; ΔG becomes negative when TΔS exceeds ΔH, or T>ΔH/ΔS in kelvin.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the inequality; (C) ignores positive enthalpy at low T; (D) ignores increasing TΔS.
Key point: Solve the inequality with the sign of ΔS fixed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: The figure gives ideal-mixture pure-component vapour pressures p*A=80 kPa and p*B=20 kPa. At liquid mole fraction xA=0.25, what is the total vapour pressure?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 35 kPa.
Given: xB=0.75 and the mixture follows Raoult's law.
Formula/Principle: p_total=xA p*A+xB p*B.
Step 1: 0.25×80+0.75×20=20+15=35 kPa.
Why: The total pressure sums component partial pressures, with liquid-phase mole fractions weighting the pure-component values. At xA=0.25, A contributes 20 kPa and B contributes 15 kPa, so neither pure-component pressure alone represents the mixture.
Why not the others: (A) uses B alone; (C) takes a simple average; (D) reverses the fractions.
Key point: Distinguish liquid composition from vapour pressure contribution.
questions.image_alt: Ideal mixture pure-component vapour pressures and composition

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A 1.0 mol mixture of methane and ethane undergoes complete combustion and produces 1.4 mol CO₂. What mole fraction of the original mixture was ethane?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.4 ethane mole fraction.
Given: Methane contributes one CO₂ per molecule and ethane two.
Formula/Principle: Let ethane fraction be x; carbon balance gives (1−x)+2x=1.4.
Step 1: 1+x=1.4, hence x=0.4. Cross-check the product is between 1 and 2 mol.
Why: The extra 0.4 mol carbon dioxide over pure methane arises from the second carbon in each ethane molecule. Oxygen supplied in combustion does not change the carbon balance.
Why not the others: (B) would yield 1.2 mol CO₂; (C) yields 1.6; (D) yields 1.8.
Key point: Use product carbon balance to infer a mixture fraction.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An optically pure (R)-2-bromobutane reacts with a strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic medium under conditions favouring a single backside SN2 displacement and no rearrangement. What is expected for substitution at the stereogenic carbon?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Inversion at the reacting centre.
Why: SN2 bond formation and leaving-group departure occur concertedly from opposite sides. The tetrahedral arrangement inverts, though the product's R/S descriptor depends on substituent priorities after substitution; the prompt asks local geometry rather than guaranteeing an S label.
Why not the others: (A) is incompatible with backside attack; (B) describes a planar intermediate route; (D) ignores the stereogenic centre.
Key point: Geometric inversion is more robust than a bare R-to-S claim.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For A=[[1,2],[2,5]], solve A(x,y)ᵀ=(3,7)ᵀ. What is x+y?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2.
Given: x+2y=3 and 2x+5y=7.
Formula/Principle: Eliminate x using the first equation.
Step 1: Subtract twice the first from the second to obtain y=1; then x=1.
Worked derivation: \[2x+5y-2(x+2y)=7-6\Rightarrow y=1,\quad x=3-2=1,\quad x+y=2.\]
Why: The elimination fixes both coordinates before their requested sum is taken. A common shortcut is to add the two right-hand-side values or read a single coordinate without checking that the pair satisfies both matrix rows.
Why not the others: (B) reports one coordinate; (C) adds one twice; (D) reports the original right-hand-side component.
Key point: Solve first, then calculate the requested expression.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Among integers 1 through 120, how many are divisible by exactly two of 2, 3 and 5?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 28.
Given: Pairwise intersection counts are floor(120/6)=20, floor(120/10)=12, floor(120/15)=8; triple intersection floor(120/30)=4.
Formula/Principle: Pairwise sum counts each exactly-two member once but each triple member three times, so subtract 3 times the triple count.
Step 1: 20+12+8−3×4=28.
Worked derivation: \[N_2=\left\lfloor\frac{120}{6}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{120}{10}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac{120}{15}\right\rfloor-3\left\lfloor\frac{120}{30}\right\rfloor=28.\]
Why: The phrase exactly two excludes every multiple of 30, which is present in all three pairwise sets. Subtracting the triple intersection only once would still count those integers twice, so the exclusion coefficient is three here.
Why not the others: (B) includes triples three times; (C) subtracts them once; (D) subtracts them four times.
Key point: Correct the multiplicity of the triple intersection.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: On integers define aRb when a−b is divisible by 4. Which statement is true about R?
options: A) Reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
B) An equivalence relation with four residue classes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Four congruence classes.
Worked derivation: \[a-a=0;\quad a-b=4k\Rightarrow b-a=-4k;\quad a-b=4k,\ b-c=4j\Rightarrow a-c=4(k+j).\]
Why: The three displayed checks establish reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity. Every integer has one residue 0,1,2,3 modulo 4, and precisely integers with equal residues are related. The four residue classes partition all integers because any integer has exactly one remainder on division by four.
Why not the others: (A) denies transitivity even though differences add; (C) denies reflexivity although a−a=0; (D) denies symmetry and transitivity despite signed and summed multiples of four.
Key point: Verify all three properties before counting classes.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The cube roots of unity are plotted on the unit complex circle. What is the area of the triangle formed by them?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3√3/4.
Given: Each pair of consecutive roots subtends a central angle of 120°.
Formula/Principle: Chord length=2sin60°=√3; equilateral area=(√3/4)s².
Step 1: Substitute s²=3.
Worked derivation: \[s=2\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt3,\qquad A=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}(\sqrt3)^2=\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}.\]
Why: The roots lie evenly spaced on a circle of radius one, so the side is the chord, not the radius. Using the distance from origin to a root as the triangle side would be wrong: the side connects two roots separated by 120°.
Why not the others: (A) doubles the area; (B) uses the wrong side; (C) uses radius as side.
Key point: Determine chord length before area.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Evaluate ∫₀² x√(4−x²) dx.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 8/3.
Given: Put u=4−x², so du=−2x dx and bounds x=0,2 map to u=4,0.
Formula/Principle: Reverse the bounds to absorb the minus sign, then integrate u¹ᐟ².
Step 1: The integral is ½∫₀⁴√u du.
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^2x\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx=\frac12\int_0^4u^{1/2}du=\frac13\left[u^{3/2}\right]_0^4=\frac83.\]
Why: The original integrand is nonnegative, so reversing the transformed limits is necessary; omitting it would give a negative area. The resulting positive 8/3 also provides a sign check against the original nonnegative curve over the given interval.
Why not the others: (A) loses a factor two; (B) uses the endpoint radius alone; (D) doubles the result.
Key point: Transform the limits and differential together.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The planes x+y+z=3 and x−y+z=1 intersect in a line. Which point lies on this line?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (1,1,1).
Given: Subtract plane equations to get 2y=2.
Formula/Principle: The line consists of y=1 and x+z=2.
Step 1: For (1,1,1), y=1 and x+z=2.
Worked derivation: \[(x+y+z)-(x-y+z)=2\Rightarrow y=1,\quad x+z=2.\]
Why: Intersection membership requires simultaneous satisfaction, not just one plane. The first plane alone admits an entire plane of candidates; only its intersection with the second reduces them to a line.
Why not the others: (B) has x+z=1; (C) has y=0; (D) has y=2.
Key point: Check both constraints for each candidate.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For f_a(x)=x³−3ax on x≥1, which real a makes f_a strictly increasing throughout its domain and makes its minimum value on the domain at most −2?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) a=1.
Given: f′_a(x)=3(x²−a); positivity for x>1 requires a≤1.
Formula/Principle: For a≤1 the minimum is at x=1, with f_a(1)=1−3a.
Step 1: Demand 1−3a≤−2, giving a≥1; intersect with a≤1.
Worked derivation: \[a\le1,\qquad 1-3a\le-2\iff a\ge1\quad\Rightarrow\quad a=1.\]
Why: At a=1 the derivative vanishes only at the left endpoint and is positive for all x>1, so the function remains strictly increasing on [1,∞). The equality case a=1 is allowed because the derivative is zero only at the endpoint and stays positive at every later x.
Why not the others: (A) loses monotonicity near 1; (C) includes values with minimum greater than −2; (D) misses equality.
Key point: Intersect a global derivative condition with a value bound.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Three observations have mean 4 and population variance 8. Two observations are 2 and 4. What is the third observation, and is the stated variance consistent?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6, inconsistent.
Given: Sum=3×4=12, so third=6; deviations from 4 are −2,0,+2.
Formula/Principle: Population variance=(sum squared deviations)/3.
Step 1: Variance=(4+0+4)/3=8/3, not 8.
Worked derivation: \[x_3=12-2-4=6,\quad \sigma^2=\frac{(2-4)^2+(4-4)^2+(6-4)^2}{3}=\frac83.\]
Why: Mean constrains the missing datum, but the variance supplies a separate consistency check. The calculated 8/3 differs from the reported 8, so no third observation can satisfy both summaries simultaneously.
Why not the others: (A) uses the mean but fails the variance test; (B) chooses 8 as the datum and falsely accepts the variance; (D) also chooses 8 and rejects variance without first satisfying the mean.
Key point: Check both reported summary statistics.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For f(x)=(x²−9)/(x−3) when x≠3, what value of f(3) makes the function continuous?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 6.
Given: x²−9=(x−3)(x+3).
Formula/Principle: Removable continuity requires f(3)=limₓ→₃f(x).
Step 1: Cancel only for x≠3, then evaluate x+3 at 3.
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{x\to3}\frac{x^2-9}{x-3}=\lim_{x\to3}(x+3)=6.\]
Why: The algebra gives the limiting value, but the original quotient remains undefined at x=3 until f(3) is explicitly assigned. This assigned point does not change any neighboring values; it only removes the discontinuity at the missing input.
Why not the others: (A) substitutes into numerator only; (B) uses x; (C) uses x².
Key point: Fill a hole with its finite limit.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A fair coin is tossed five times. What is the probability of exactly three heads given that the first toss was a head?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3/8.
Given: With the first head fixed, four independent tosses remain.
Formula/Principle: Exactly two heads among four has C(4,2) favourable sequences out of 2⁴.
Step 1: 6/16=3/8.
Worked derivation: \[P(H_{\rm total}=3\mid H_1)=\binom42(1/2)^4=\frac38.\]
Why: Conditioning changes the sample space; the first head already contributes one of the required three. Among the remaining four tosses, exactly two heads and two tails are needed; that is why the combination count is six rather than ten.
Why not the others: (A) undercounts; (B) is the unconditional probability; (D) ignores the exact-count restriction.
Key point: Reduce both required successes and remaining trials.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Find the sum of all distinct x in the closed interval [0,2π] satisfying sin x+cos x=1.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 5π/2.
Given: Write sin x+cos x=√2 sin(x+π/4).
Formula/Principle: Solve sin(x+π/4)=1/√2 over a full closed period.
Step 1: x=0, π/2 and 2π are the distinct solutions in [0,2π].
Worked derivation: \[\sum x=0+\frac\pi2+2\pi=\frac{5\pi}{2}.\]
Why: Both endpoints represent different real x values and satisfy the equation, though their trig states are the same; a half-open interval would omit one. Summing roots rather than merely counting them makes the 2π endpoint contribute to the answer even though it shares a sine/cosine state with zero.
Why not the others: (A) omits 2π; (C) omits π/2; (D) loses one endpoint and adds an unrelated angle.
Key point: Respect the specified closed interval when summing roots.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For x>0, solve y′+(1/x)y=x with y(1)=0. What is y(2)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 7/6.
Given: Integrating factor for y′+y/x is x.
Formula/Principle: Multiply through by x to obtain (xy)′=x².
Step 1: xy=x³/3+C; at x=1, y=0 implies C=−1/3.
Worked derivation: \[xy=\frac{x^3-1}{3}\Rightarrow y(2)=\frac{2^3-1}{3\cdot2}=\frac76.\]
Why: The nonconstant coefficient changes the integrating factor; simply solving with a constant exponential transient would not satisfy the differential equation. Multiplying by x is valid because the domain excludes zero; it turns both left-hand terms into the derivative of xy.
Why not the others: (B) omits division by x; (C) loses the cubic contribution; (D) uses the wrong initial constant.
Key point: Check the integrating factor before integrating.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For x²−kx+9=0 to have two distinct positive real roots, which condition on real k is necessary and sufficient?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) k>6.
Given: Root product=9>0 and sum=k.
Formula/Principle: Distinct real roots require k²−36>0; positivity requires sum k>0.
Step 1: Intersect k>0 with k>6 or k<−6 to obtain k>6.
Worked derivation: \[k^2-36>0,\ k>0\iff k>6.\]
Why: Positive product alone could mean two negative roots; the positive sum excludes that possibility, and strict discriminant excludes a repeated root. The two inequalities have different jobs: the discriminant creates distinct real roots and the positive sum chooses the positive pair rather than two negatives.
Why not the others: (A) permits complex roots; (B) includes a double root; (C) gives negative roots.
Key point: Combine discriminant, sum and product.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: At the point (1,2) on y²=4x, what is the slope of the normal?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) −1.
Given: Differentiate y²=4x implicitly.
Formula/Principle: Tangent slope=2/y=1 at y=2; normal is negative reciprocal.
Step 1: Normal slope=−1.
Worked derivation: \[2y\frac{dy}{dx}=4\Rightarrow m_t=\frac2y=1,\quad m_n=-\frac1{m_t}=-1.\]
Why: A normal is perpendicular to the tangent, so use the negative reciprocal of its slope. Evaluating the tangent slope at the specified point is essential before taking its perpendicular direction; the symbolic slope varies along the parabola.
Why not the others: (A) omits the reciprocal after an incorrect tangent slope; (B) loses sign; (D) is tangent.
Key point: Differentiate first, then take negative reciprocal.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For a=(2,−1,2) and b=(1,2,2), what is the scalar projection of a onto b?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 4/3.
Given: a·b=2−2+4=4 and norm b=3.
Formula/Principle: Scalar projection of a on b is (a·b)/norm b.
Step 1: 4/3.
Worked derivation: \[\operatorname{comp}_{b}a=\frac{a\cdot b}{\lVert b\rVert}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{1+4+4}}=\frac43.\]
Why: Dividing by norm b once gives the signed length along b; dividing by its square would give a vector coefficient instead. The projection is positive because the dot product is positive; using norm squared would instead give the coefficient in the vector projection formula.
Why not the others: (A) is dot product; (C) doubles it; (D) is norm b.
Key point: Scalar and vector projection use different denominators.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line / Motion in a Plane
questions.question: The acceleration-time graph shows a=+2 m s⁻² from 0 to 2 s and a=−1 m s⁻² from 2 to 6 s. A particle begins at 3 m s⁻¹. What is v at 6 s?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3 m s⁻¹.
Given: Initial velocity 3; signed acceleration areas are 2×2 and −1×4.
Formula/Principle: Δv=∫a dt, signed area under a-t plot.
Step 1: Net Δv=4−4=0.
Worked derivation: \[v(6)=3+(2)(2)+(-1)(4)=3\ {\rm m\,s^{-1}}.\]
Why: Opposite acceleration intervals cancel velocity change, even though distance travelled cannot be inferred from net area alone. The graph has a larger positive acceleration for a shorter interval and a smaller negative acceleration for longer; their areas, not their heights, cancel.
Why not the others: (B) ignores first interval; (C) drops initial velocity; (D) ignores negative area.
Key point: Use signed acceleration area.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 0.5 kg block descends 0.4 m without friction and compresses a horizontal spring of k=100 N m⁻¹. What is its maximum compression? Take g=10 m s⁻² and neglect height change during compression.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 0.20 m.
Given: Lost gravitational potential is mgh=2 J.
Formula/Principle: At maximum compression, kinetic energy is zero and ½kx²=mgh.
Step 1: 50x²=2 so x=0.20 m.
Worked derivation: \[x=\sqrt{2mgh/k}=\sqrt{(2)(0.5)(10)(0.4)/100}=0.20\ {\rm m}.\]
Why: Energy is conserved across the descent and compression; taking the square root is required after equating potential energies. At maximum compression the block pauses, so no kinetic energy term remains; the horizontal travel was stipulated not to change gravitational potential.
Why not the others: (A) halves x; (C) equates height with compression; (D) misuses spring energy.
Key point: State the reference and final zero-speed condition.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: The same constant torque acts on two rigid rotors with moments of inertia I and 4I. What is the ratio of their angular accelerations α₁/α₂?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 4.
Given: Equal net torque τ; second rotor has four times inertia.
Formula/Principle: τ=Iα.
Step 1: α₁=τ/I, α₂=τ/(4I).
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\alpha_1}{\alpha_2}=\frac{\tau/I}{\tau/(4I)}=4.\]
Why: Moment of inertia resists angular acceleration for a specified torque, so multiplying inertia by four divides acceleration by four. This inverse dependence assumes the same net torque, which is why the ratio is four rather than a comparison of rotational kinetic energies.
Why not the others: (A) inverts ratio; (B) takes square root; (D) squares it.
Key point: Specify which rotor is numerator.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two small spheres of equal density fall through the same viscous liquid at low Reynolds number. Sphere B has twice the radius of A. Neglect boundary effects. What is their terminal-speed ratio vB/vA?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4.
Given: Driving net weight ∝r³; Stokes drag at terminal speed ∝rv.
Formula/Principle: 6πηrv=(4π/3)r³(ρs−ρl)g.
Step 1: v∝r² under unchanged viscosity and density contrast.
Worked derivation: \[v_t=\frac{2(\rho_s-\rho_l)gr^2}{9\eta},\quad \frac{v_B}{v_A}=\left(\frac{2r_A}{r_A}\right)^2=4.\]
Why: Larger spheres have more excess weight per unit linear drag; this scaling applies only in the assumed Stokes regime. If the radius change made the Reynolds number large, Stokes drag would fail; the problem explicitly restricts the regime to preserve the quadratic scaling.
Why not the others: (A) reverses and squares; (B) reverses; (C) uses a linear radius law.
Key point: Derive terminal speed from force balance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An ideal gas expands adiabatically and reversibly from state 1 to state 2. Which combination is correct for work done by the gas, internal-energy change and heat transfer?
options: A) Positive work, negative ΔU, zero heat
B) Positive work, positive ΔU, zero heat
C) Zero work, zero ΔU, positive heat
D) Negative work, negative ΔU, positive heat
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Work draws from internal energy.
Worked derivation: \[Q=0,\quad \Delta U=Q-W=-W<0\quad (W>0).\]
Why: Adiabatic means no heat exchange, not constant temperature. In a reversible expansion, the gas does positive work and therefore cools as its internal energy decreases.
Why not the others: (B) violates first law; (C) implies no expansion; (D) reverses work sign and adds heat.
Key point: Declare work sign convention.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A tuning fork makes 4 beats per second with a 250 Hz reference. When the reference frequency is increased to 252 Hz, beat frequency falls to 2 Hz. What is the fork frequency?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 254 Hz.
Given: First observation gives possible fork frequencies 246 or 254 Hz.
Formula/Principle: Beat frequency is the magnitude of frequency difference.
Step 1: Against 252 Hz, 254 yields 2 beats whereas 246 yields 6.
Worked derivation: \[|f-250|=4\Rightarrow f\in\{246,254\};\quad |f-252|=2\Rightarrow f=254.\]
Why: One beat rate alone has an above/below ambiguity; changing the reference resolves it by a second constraint. The second reference is closer to 254 Hz but farther from 246 Hz, so the observed beat reduction selects the higher candidate.
Why not the others: (A) yields 6 second beats; (C) fails first; (D) yields zero second beats.
Key point: Intersect both absolute-value conditions.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A satellite changes from a circular orbit of radius r to a circular orbit of radius 4r about the same planet. What is the new orbital period divided by the old one?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 8.
Given: Central mass and G remain fixed.
Formula/Principle: Circular orbit balance yields T∝r³ᐟ².
Step 1: (4r/r)³ᐟ²=4³ᐟ²=8.
Worked derivation: \[T=2\pi\sqrt{\frac{r^3}{GM}},\quad \frac{T_2}{T_1}=\sqrt{4^3}=8.\]
Why: The orbiting speed also changes, so the period cannot be inferred from circumference ratio alone. Force balance gives speed proportional to r⁻¹ᐟ², which combines with a circumference proportional to r to produce period proportional to r³ᐟ².
Why not the others: (A) square-root ratio; (B) circumference ratio; (D) squares radius ratio.
Key point: Use Kepler scaling derived from force balance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: The graph gives Ex=+E₀ between x=0 and a and Ex=−2E₀ between x=a and 2a. What is V(2a)−V(0)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) +E₀a.
Given: Signed field area is E₀a−2E₀a=−E₀a.
Formula/Principle: Potential change ΔV=−∫Ex dx.
Step 1: Negate the signed area to obtain +E₀a.
Worked derivation: \[V(2a)-V(0)=-[E_0a-2E_0a]=+E_0a.\]
Why: A field pointing toward −x in the second region makes potential increase as x increases there; its larger magnitude dominates the first interval. The negative-field segment contributes twice the potential rise produced by the positive-field segment's drop, leaving a net positive change.
Why not the others: (B) forgets final negative; (C) adds magnitudes and reverses sign; (D) adds magnitudes.
Key point: Integrate the signed field then negate.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A parallel-plate capacitor remains connected to an ideal constant-voltage battery. Its plate gap is doubled without changing area or dielectric. What is the ratio of final to initial stored energy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 1/2.
Given: Battery fixes V, and C=εA/d.
Formula/Principle: U=½CV²; doubling d halves C.
Step 1: Uf/Ui=Cf/Ci=1/2.
Worked derivation: \[C_f=\frac{\epsilon A}{2d}=\frac{C_i}{2},\quad \frac{U_f}{U_i}=\frac{C_fV^2/2}{C_iV^2/2}=\frac12.\]
Why: Charge flows back into the battery as capacitance falls; using fixed charge would answer a different boundary condition. Because voltage stays fixed during the mechanical change, the energy ratio follows capacitance linearly; an isolated capacitor would obey a different law.
Why not the others: (A) assumes fixed charge; (B) squares distance; (C) squares capacitance.
Key point: Identify which electrical quantity the battery holds fixed.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A 12 V cell with internal resistance 1 Ω drives an external 5 Ω resistor. What is its terminal voltage under load?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 10 V.
Given: Total series resistance 6 Ω.
Formula/Principle: Current I=E/(R+r), terminal voltage V=E−Ir=IR.
Step 1: I=2 A; V=12−2×1=10 V.
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac{12}{5+1}=2\ {\rm A},\quad V=IR=(2)(5)=10\ {\rm V}.\]
Why: Terminal voltage is lower than open-circuit emf when current flows because internal resistance consumes part of the emf. The 2 V internal drop is not the delivered voltage; the external 5 Ω resistor receives the remaining 10 V at 2 A.
Why not the others: (A) adds internal drop; (B) ignores internal loss; (C) is internal drop.
Key point: Use total resistance for current.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Moving Charges and Magnetism / Magnetism and Matter
questions.question: Two long parallel wires carry steady currents in the same direction. If the separation doubles but currents remain unchanged, what happens to force per unit length?
options: B) It halves, and the force remains attractive
C) It quarters and becomes repulsive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Half, still attractive.
Worked derivation: \[\frac FL=\frac{\mu_0I_1I_2}{2\pi d}\Rightarrow (F/L)_{2d}=\frac12(F/L)_d.\]
Why: Same-direction currents attract; doubling only separation changes inverse-distance magnitude, not current directions or force sense. The attraction can also be seen from each wire's field acting on the other's current, with the separation entering the field magnitude inversely.
Why not the others: (A) reverses scaling; (C) uses square-law and changes sign; (D) ignores distance.
Key point: Magnetic line force scales as 1/d.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: In a series RLC circuit driven at variable frequency, the resistance is increased while L and C stay fixed. Which change is expected near resonance in the current-versus-frequency curve?
options: A) A sharper and taller peak
B) The resonance frequency necessarily doubles
C) A lower, broader current peak
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Lower, broader peak.
Worked derivation: \[\omega_0=\frac1{\sqrt{LC}},\quad I_{\max}=\frac{V}{R},\quad Q=\frac{\omega_0L}{R}.\]
Why: Increasing R lowers maximum current and quality factor; the reduced Q broadens the resonance around the same ideal LC frequency. The same driving voltage divided by a larger R gives less peak current, while greater damping spreads appreciable response over a wider band.
Why not the others: (A) reverses damping; (B) changes LC without changing either; (D) ignores finite R.
Key point: Resistance controls damping, while LC sets ideal resonance.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: The prism sketch shows a ray passing symmetrically: angle of incidence equals angle of emergence and the prism apex angle is 60°. If incidence is 50°, what is the deviation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 40°.
Given: i=e=50°, apex A=60°.
Formula/Principle: Prism deviation δ=i+e−A.
Step 1: 50+50−60=40°.
Worked derivation: \[\delta=i+e-A=50^\circ+50^\circ-60^\circ=40^\circ.\]
Why: Symmetric passage gives equal entry and exit angles, but their sum must still be reduced by the prism apex. The sketch identifies angles relative to the normals.
Why not the others: (A) halves the incidence sum; (C) uses A/2; (D) equates deviation with incidence.
Key point: Label angles against surface normals.
questions.image_alt: Prism ray and surface normal angles

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two photons have wavelengths 400 nm and 600 nm in vacuum. What is the ratio f₄₀₀/f₆₀₀?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3/2.
Given: Both photons travel at c in vacuum.
Formula/Principle: f=c/λ, so frequency is inverse to wavelength.
Step 1: f400/f600=600/400=3/2.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{f_{400}}{f_{600}}=\frac{c/(400\,\mathrm{nm})}{c/(600\,\mathrm{nm})}=\frac{600}{400}=\frac32.\]
Why: The shorter wavelength photon has higher frequency; the wave speed cancels in the ratio. A factor 3/2 in frequency follows from the inverse ratio of wavelengths; photon energy would have that same ratio but is not squared.
Why not the others: (A) reverses ratio; (B) treats frequencies equal; (D) squares inverse-wavelength ratio.
Key point: Frequency is inversely proportional to wavelength.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two independent radioactive isotopes A and B start with equal activities. Their half-lives are 1 h and 2 h respectively. What is the ratio of total activity after 2 h to initial total activity?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3/8.
Given: A retains 1/4 activity and B retains 1/2 after two hours.
Formula/Principle: Activities add; initial A₀=B₀.
Step 1: Final=(A₀/4+A₀/2)=3A₀/4; initial=2A₀.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{A(2)+B(2)}{A(0)+B(0)}=\frac{A_0(1/4+1/2)}{2A_0}=\frac38.\]
Why: Equal initial activities, not equal nuclei counts, set the weighting. Different half-lives make their remaining fractions unequal.
Why not the others: (A) uses A only; (B) uses B only; (C) sums fractions without correct initial normalization.
Key point: Weight decay fractions by initial activities.
